## AI-generated Overview (from reference literature and SuttaCentral)
*This overview was drafted by an AI model from the cited scholarship and SuttaCentral data and may contain errors; verify against the sources before relying on it.*
The *Bakajātaka* (Ja 236) is a narrative belonging to the Jātaka collection of the Pali canon [SuttaCentral]. According to the prose commentary, the Buddha delivered the story while dwelling at Jetavana in connection with a hypocritical monk, remarking that the monk had similarly been a hypocrite in a past existence [SuttaCentral; Fausböll 1879]. In the story of the past, the Bodhisatta was reborn as the leader or king of the fish (*maccharājā*) in a pond [Fausböll 1879; Söhnen-Thieme]. A crane (*baka*), seeking to prey upon the fish, assumes a deceptively tranquil posture—drooping its head, spreading its wings, and looking vacantly into the water [Söhnen-Thieme]. While the other fish are initially taken in by the bird's feigned harmlessness, the Bodhisatta perceives the predator's true intentions and warns them, prompting the fish to splash water and drive the crane away [Fausböll 1879; Söhnen-Thieme]. The Buddha concludes the tale by identifying the hypocrite monk with the crane and himself with the fish king [Fausböll 1879].
SuttaCentral records four translations across four languages and lists no direct parallels [SuttaCentral]. Computational analyses in DharmaNexus likewise report no Pali-internal text reuse or cross-language matches meeting the retrieval threshold [DharmaNexus]. However, comparative studies note that this story belongs to a broader Indian narrative cycle concerning hypocritical animals, sharing half a *gāthā* with the *Dhammaddhajajātaka* as well as thematic parallels with fables found in the *Mahābhārata* [Söhnen-Thieme].
